sections.heading: Strong inside, weak outside
sections.text:
In a simple covalent substance, each molecule is held together by strong covalent bonds. But the molecules attract one another only weakly.
When the substance melts or boils, only these weak forces between molecules are overcome; the molecules themselves stay whole.
So little energy is needed: oxygen, carbon dioxide and methane are gases; water and ethanol are liquids; wax, sugar and iodine are soft solids.

sections.heading: No conduction
sections.text:
To conduct, a substance needs charged particles that can move. Molecular substances have neither ions nor free electrons, so they do not conduct when solid, liquid or dissolved.
That is why plastics, which are covalent, are used to insulate electric wires.

sections.heading: Solubility, and an important exception
sections.text:
Many covalent substances do not dissolve in water but do dissolve in organic solvents such as kerosene, petrol or ethanol (grease on hands is removed with kerosene). Some, like sugar and ethanol, dissolve in water.
Not all covalent substances are molecular: diamond, graphite and sand (silicon dioxide) are giant covalent structures with very high melting points. You will meet them in a later lesson.

key_words.meaning: a carbon-based liquid such as kerosene or ethanol

examples: Iodine: soft, turns to vapour easily
Sugar: dissolves in water, solution does not conduct

mistake.wrong: When water boils, the O–H bonds break
mistake.right: When water boils, the molecules separate; the O–H bonds stay
mistake.why: Steam is still H₂O: only the weak forces between molecules are overcome.

worked_example.problem: Explain why water boils at {100} °C while sodium chloride boils at about {1400} °C.
steps: Boiling water only separates the molecules from one another; the forces between molecules are weak.
Boiling salt means separating ions held by strong ionic bonds throughout the lattice.
Much less energy is needed for water.
worked_example.answer: Weak forces between water molecules; strong ionic bonds in salt

cards.idea: Weak forces between molecules: low melting and boiling points.
example: Carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature.

cards.idea: Molecular substances do not conduct: there are no free charged particles.
example: Pure water and sugar solution conduct very poorly.

cards.idea: Many dissolve in organic solvents rather than water.
example: Candle wax dissolves in kerosene, not in water.

pick.q: Candle wax is put in kerosene and in water. Where does it dissolve?
e: Wax is covalent and insoluble in water.
It does not dissolve in water.
pick.y: Covalent substances often dissolve in organic solvents.

pick.q: Which covalent substance dissolves well in water?
pick.y: Some covalent molecules, such as sugar and ethanol, dissolve in water.

pick.q: Iodine crystals are soft and turn into vapour on gentle heating. This shows that…
pick.r: the forces between iodine molecules are weak
e: Ionic solids are hard with high melting points.
The molecules stay as I₂; it is the forces between them that are weak.
pick.y: Little energy is needed to separate the molecules.

pick.q: Why does carbon dioxide have a low boiling point?
pick.r: The forces between its molecules are weak
w: The bonds inside the molecule are weak
e: The covalent bonds inside are strong; they do not break when it boils.
pick.y: Boiling separates molecules, which are weakly attracted.

pick.q: Which is most likely a simple covalent substance?
w: a solid that conducts when molten
e: That is typical of an ionic compound.
pick.y: Low boiling point: weak forces between molecules (ethanol).

pick.q: When ice melts, what is broken?
pick.r: the weak forces between water molecules
e: The molecules stay whole: still H₂O.
Nuclei are never broken in melting.

pick.q: Why does sugar solution not conduct electricity?
pick.r: Sugar is made of molecules with no charge
e: Salt water conducts, so water is not the problem.
Free electrons would make it conduct.
pick.y: No ions are formed when sugar dissolves.

pick.q: Which substance does not conduct electricity when molten?
pick.y: Wax has neither ions nor free electrons.

pick.q: Pure water conducts very poorly. Why?
pick.r: It is made of covalent molecules with almost no ions
e: Water is a liquid at room temperature.
pick.y: Without moving ions there is almost no current.

pick.q: Candle wax is put in kerosene and in water. Where does it dissolve?
e: Wax is covalent and insoluble in water.
It does not dissolve in water.
pick.y: Covalent substances often dissolve in organic solvents.

pick.q: Which covalent substance dissolves well in water?
pick.y: Some covalent molecules, such as sugar and ethanol, dissolve in water.

pick.q: Iodine crystals are soft and turn into vapour on gentle heating. This shows that…
pick.r: the forces between iodine molecules are weak
e: Ionic solids are hard with high melting points.
The molecules stay as I₂; it is the forces between them that are weak.
pick.y: Little energy is needed to separate the molecules.

pick.q: Substance A melts at 801 °C and conducts when molten. Substance B melts at 0 °C and does not conduct. Which is covalent?
e: A conducts when molten, so it is ionic.
B has the properties of a molecular substance.
pick.y: Low melting point and no conduction: covalent molecules.

pick.q: Sand (silicon dioxide) is covalent but melts at about 1700 °C. Why?
pick.r: It is a giant covalent structure: many strong bonds must break
w: It is made of small molecules
pick.y: Giant covalent lattices have very high melting points.

pick.q: Which statement about simple covalent substances is FALSE?
e: True: the covalent bonds themselves are strong.
pick.y: They have no ions or free electrons, so they do not conduct.
